source: a16z Podcast — AI demand outrunning compute supply; frontier-lab revenue is self-determined, reinvestment math, not necessarily winner-take-all
summary: The future of enterprise AI is a hybrid/multi-model architecture — own fine-tuned open-source model plus one or two frontier models behind a router — not a single dominant frontier model
summary_extended: Baker argues that the future enterprise AI architecture will be a hybrid/multi-model ensemble — enterprises will take the best available open-source base model (likely an Nvidia-developed model given its Poolside acquisition), apply reinforcement learning and supervised fine-tuning on their own proprietary data, and then route tasks to frontier models (e.g., Gemini, Grok, Claude) only for high-level planning while using the owned, fine-tuned model for execution. His core reasoning is that sharing proprietary enterprise context with frontier labs is 'hazardous for financial health,' particularly as zero-data-retention policy shifts make this riskier, creating a structural incentive for enterprises to own and control their own intelligence layer. Baker cites real-world instantiations already emerging — Grockbot using Gemini 3.7 Flash plus Grok 4.6 plus Opus behind a router, as well as Cursor, Harvey, and Fireworks Nexus — as evidence this architecture is not theoretical but already in production. The investment implication is that this is bullish for Microsoft (as an enterprise AI platform and distribution layer), application software companies that can embed proprietary workflows, and potentially Nvidia (whose open-source model could become the dominant fine-tuning base), while being structurally negative for pure frontier model providers who depend on deep enterprise data access and lock-in.
